And take responsibility for the final decision.

My lesson: Never confuse an articulate answer with a validated business decision.

4. Using AI to Create More Work Instead of Eliminating Work

This one is particularly interesting.

AI promises to reduce work.

But sometimes it does the opposite.

Let me explain.

Suppose you're managing a small company.

You introduce several AI tools.

One for research.

One for content.

One for project management.

One for automation.

One for presentations.

One for customer communication.

Initially, everything feels faster.

But gradually, you begin managing the tools themselves.

Different subscriptions.

Different interfaces.

Different workflows.

Different files.

Different outputs that need reviewing.

You saved time performing individual tasks.

But you created another layer of work coordinating the tools.

This is a mistake founders should watch carefully.

Every additional system introduces some amount of complexity.

And complexity has a cost.

Sometimes the best way to improve productivity isn't adding another AI tool.

It's removing an unnecessary task.

Before automating a process, I now prefer asking:

"Does this process need to exist at all?"

Because eliminating unnecessary work is often more valuable than automating it.

5. Believing Faster Execution Automatically Creates Competitive Advantage

AI has made execution dramatically more accessible.

That's exciting, especially for founders operating with limited resources.

You no longer need a large team to prototype every idea.

You can research faster.

Build faster.

Write faster.

Experiment faster.

But there's another side to this development.

If everyone can build faster, speed alone becomes a weaker advantage.

Imagine two startups building similar products.

Both use AI coding assistants.

Both can create working prototypes quickly.

Both have access to similar infrastructure and models.

Where does the differentiation come from?

It may come from understanding a customer problem more deeply.

Having better distribution.

Building trust.

Creating a superior experience.

Developing strong industry relationships.

Or making better product decisions.

AI can reduce the cost of execution.

It cannot automatically create customer trust or a meaningful market position.

This is why I believe founders need to think beyond productivity.

The important question isn't simply:

"How much faster can we build?"

It's:

"Why would someone choose what we're building?"

That question becomes even more important when competitors have access to the same powerful tools.

6. Forgetting That Human Relationships Still Build Businesses

As AI capabilities improve, it becomes tempting to automate every interaction.

Customer emails.

Sales outreach.

Follow-ups.

Social media conversations.

Networking messages.

Even parts of relationship management.

Some automation is genuinely helpful.

But there's something I don't want founders to overlook.

Businesses are still built on trust between people.

An AI-generated message can be grammatically perfect.

It can sound professional.

It can even be personalized.

But that doesn't mean it establishes a meaningful relationship.

Think about receiving a message from someone who clearly understands your work, references an idea you've shared, and asks a thoughtful question.

Now compare it with a polished message that could have been sent to five hundred people.

Both might be professionally written.

Only one makes you feel that someone is genuinely interested.

As a founder, I believe relationships are one of the few advantages that cannot be replicated simply by subscribing to another AI service.

AI can help us prepare.

It can help us research.

It can help us communicate more clearly.

But the intention behind the relationship must remain human.

My lesson: Use AI to support relationships, not to replace the effort required to build them.

7. Asking AI for Too Many Answers and Not Spending Enough Time Thinking

This may be the most personal lesson of all.

AI makes getting answers incredibly easy.

Have an idea?

Ask AI.

Facing a difficult decision?

Ask AI.

Need a strategy?

Ask AI.

Don't know what to do next?

Ask AI.

There's nothing inherently wrong with any of this.

The danger appears when we stop developing our own point of view.

As a founder, I don't think our most important job is collecting answers.

It's making decisions under uncertainty.

And that requires independent judgment.

AI can provide five options.

It can compare advantages and disadvantages.

It can identify risks.

It can challenge our assumptions.

But eventually, someone has to decide.

Sometimes there won't be enough information.

Sometimes the market will behave unpredictably.

Sometimes an apparently logical decision will fail.

And sometimes the unconventional decision will turn out to be the right one.

That's the reality of entrepreneurship.

I don't want AI to eliminate that responsibility.

I want it to help me become better at handling it.

One useful way to do this is to form an opinion before consulting AI.

Instead of asking:

"What should I do?"

Try:

"Here is my current reasoning. What assumptions am I missing? What evidence would prove me wrong?"

It's a small change.

But it moves AI from being an answer generator to being a tool for examining decisions.

And I think that's a much healthier relationship.

What I Would Do Differently

If I were establishing an AI-driven workflow as a founder today, I would begin with a much simpler approach.

First, identify the three most important problems affecting the business.

Not thirty.

Three.

Then examine which of those problems genuinely benefit from AI.

For each one, I would define:

  • The outcome: What should improve?
  • The baseline: How well are we doing today?
  • The approach: What is the simplest useful solution?
  • The human role: Who remains responsible for the decision?
  • The measurement: How will we know whether it helped?

Only then would I begin selecting tools and building workflows.

For example, if the problem is slow customer research, the objective shouldn't be generating fifty research reports every week.

It should be improving the quality and speed of decisions made using that research.

If the problem is customer support, the goal shouldn't be increasing the number of AI-generated responses.

It should be helping customers resolve issues accurately and efficiently.

And if the problem is content marketing, the objective shouldn't be publishing as many articles as possible.

It should be reaching the right audience, earning trust, and generating meaningful conversations.

These distinctions may sound obvious.

But AI's ability to produce so much so quickly makes them surprisingly easy to forget.

The Founder Still Has to Be the Founder

Here's something I believe strongly.

AI can be an extraordinary assistant.

It can help us think.

Research.

Create.

Analyze.

Build.

Experiment.

And sometimes accomplish things that would previously have been beyond our resources.

But it cannot take ownership of our company.

It cannot fully understand the weight of every decision.

It cannot personally build trust with our customers.

It cannot assume responsibility when a strategic bet fails.

And it cannot decide what kind of company we ultimately want to create.

Those responsibilities remain with the founder.

The more powerful AI becomes, the more important it is to remember that distinction.

The Biggest Mistake Would Be Learning Nothing

I don't regret exploring AI.

I don't regret experimenting with new tools.

And I certainly don't believe founders should avoid taking risks with emerging technology.

Experimentation is how we discover opportunities.

But experimentation should teach us something.

If a tool doesn't improve the business, we should be willing to stop using it.

If a workflow creates unnecessary complexity, we should simplify it.

If an AI-generated recommendation doesn't survive scrutiny, we should reject it.

And if an entire project begins drifting away from the actual customer problem, we should have the courage to reconsider it.

That's not being anti-AI.

That's being responsible for the business.

The more I think about entrepreneurship in the AI era, the more I come back to one conclusion:

AI can help founders do more. But knowing what deserves to be done is still the founder's job.

And perhaps that's the biggest lesson of all.

The goal isn't to build an AI-powered company simply because AI is available.

The goal is to build a valuable company and use AI wherever it genuinely helps.

Because at the end of the day, customers don't care how many AI tools we use.

They care whether we solve their problems.

And no amount of automation can replace that responsibility.

A question for fellow founders and builders:

What's one mistake you've made while using AI to build a product, run a business, or manage your work?

Was it trusting the output too much, adopting too many tools, building something nobody needed—or something completely different?

I'd love to learn from your experience.

title: ما الوظائف التي تتمنون جمعها في تطبيق الطرفية الذي تستخدمونه كل يوم؟ تجربة بناء xtty لنظام macOS
summary:
مرحبًا، أنا مطوّر xtty. أستخدم الطرفية يوميًا في البرمجة والعمل على الخوادم، وكنت أجد نفسي أكرر خطوات صغيرة كلما انتقلت بين اتصالات SSH أو احتجت إلى جلسة ثانية. بعض الأدوات الموجودة تنفّذ جزءًا مما أحتاجه، لكنني أردت أن تجتمع سير العمل التي أستخدمها باستمرار في مكان واحد، من دون إعداد طويل كل مرة.

بنيت xtty كتطبيق طرفية أصلي لنظام macOS. الفكرة ليست إضافة أكبر عدد ممكن من الخصائص، بل أن تكون الأدوات اليومية في متناول اليد حين تحتاج إليها.

هذه أمثلة من الاستخدام الفعلي:

  • فتح عدة خوادم SSH محفوظة معًا، بما فيها الاتصالات التي تستخدم jump hosts.
  • إنشاء اتصال SSH جديد ومستقل بالخادم والمجلد البعيد نفسيهما عند استخدام Duplicate Tab؛ من دون نسخ العملية الجارية أو استبدال أدوات مثل tmux.
  • تنظيم الجلسات في تبويبات وأجزاء مقسّمة، وإرسال الإدخال إلى الأجزاء التي يحددها المستخدم فقط.
  • تعبئة مطالبات كلمات المرور المعروفة من macOS Keychain.
  • نقل الملفات من الجلسة البعيدة باستخدام rz وsz مع حوارات macOS الأصلية.
  • متابعة حالات جلسات Claude Code وCodex لمعرفة أي جلسة تعمل أو انتهت أو تحتاج إلى انتباه.

لم أرد تحويل الطرفية إلى صندوق يحتوي مئات الأدوات، ولا إلى مجموعة قوالب جامدة. المضيفون والتبويبات والأجزاء ومجموعات الإدخال ونقل الملفات ومؤشرات الحالة هي مكونات بسيطة يمكن لكل شخص تركيبها وفق عمله.

حتى تكون الصورة واضحة: xtty متاح حاليًا لـ macOS 15 أو أحدث بنسختين لأجهزة Apple Silicon وIntel. يمكن استخدام الطرفية المحلية واتصالات SSH القائمة في النسخة المجانية. أما الخوادم المحفوظة وفتحها دفعة واحدة وDuplicate Tab والملء التلقائي لكلمة المرور ونقل الملفات فهي من خصائص Pro. توجد تجربة لمدة سبعة أيام من دون بطاقة، وشراء اختياري لمرة واحدة بقيمة 29.90 دولارًا بدل الاشتراك.

هذا فيديو يعرض واجهة التطبيق الحقيقية ببيانات تجريبية:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rkQMSY82Ow8

الموقع والتنزيل:
https://xtty.sh/

سؤالي لمن يستخدم macOS في التطوير أو إدارة الأنظمة: ما الخطوات الصغيرة التي تكررونها كل يوم في الطرفية، وما الوظائف التي تتمنون أن تعمل معًا من دون إعداد إضافي؟ أرحّب بالملاحظات النقدية أيضًا.
